clips.title: What is an Activity in Temporal? | Explainer Series
clips.why: A short reminder of what an activity is: the part of a workflow that talks to the outside world, and that Temporal retries when it fails.
look: Activities are where calls to other systems belong.
Temporal retries a failed activity for you.
Why that makes it important that an activity can run more than once.
clips.after: acquireSandbox, workInSandbox and releaseSandbox are activities, so each one must be safe when Temporal retries it.

clips.title: Temporal Explained • Idempotence
clips.why: The definition of idempotence and of an idempotency key, the value that lets a repeated request be recognised.
look: Two inserts with a new key each time give two records: our naive claim gives two VMs.
An idempotency key lets the receiver recognise a repeat.
The run ID tag on the VM is our idempotency key for the claim.
clips.after: The claim's first lookup, for a VM tagged with this run's ID, is how a retry recognises its own earlier attempt.
clips.quote: An idempotency key is a unique value

clips.title: The 4 Types of Timeouts in Temporal
clips.why: The heartbeat timeout is how Temporal notices within minutes that the worker following a long activity has died, and starts the retry this lesson prepares for.
look: A long activity reports heartbeats while it works.
Missing heartbeats make Temporal give up on the attempt and retry it.
The heartbeat can carry progress, so the retry knows where to continue.
clips.after: workInSandbox heartbeats every 30 seconds while it follows the harness, and a retry re-attaches to the harness that is still running.

practice.q: Complete the first line of acquireSandbox, the check that makes a retry return the VM an earlier attempt already took.
practice.hint: The tag the claim writes on the VM it takes.
practice.why: The tag lives in AWS, so it survives the worker that died, and the retry can find it.

practice.q: Why does workInSandbox start the harness as a systemd unit instead of running it as one long SSM command?

options.text: SSM commands have a deadline of at most 48 hours, and a run has no time limit
options.why: The command only starts the unit; systemd keeps the harness alive for as long as the work takes.
Speed is not the reason. The reason is that a command has a deadline and a run does not.

options.text: SSM cannot run commands as the agent user
options.why: It can, but that does not solve the deadline.

practice.q: Put one VM's life through the activities in order.
items: acquireSandbox detaches a warm VM and tags it with the run ID and a lease
freshenSandbox brings it to the run's commit and redoes only what changed
workInSandbox starts the harness unit and follows its heartbeats
parkSandbox stops it while the run waits for a person, and wakeSandbox starts it on the answer
releaseSandbox revokes the scope and terminates it from the workflow's finally block
practice.why: Claim, prepare, work, wait cheaply, and always release, with every step safe to repeat.

practice.q: The harness on a VM has sent no heartbeat for five minutes. What does workInSandbox do?

options.text: Throws SandboxDead, which Temporal does not retry, so the workflow decides what happens next
options.why: A dead VM is not fixed by running the same activity again; the workflow replaces the VM and resumes from the last checkpoint.

options.text: Keeps waiting, because runs have no time limit
options.why: No time limit on work is not the same as waiting forever for a machine that stopped answering.

options.text: Starts a second harness on the same VM
options.why: The VM itself is probably gone or frozen; a second harness would not help.
